The Great Principle (mahat), the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the five subtle elements (tanmātra)—which are designated as the unmanifest (avyakta)—are denoted by the term "the Great" (mahat). The intellect (buddhi) belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha is called by that name. Primordial Matter (pradhāna) is the root, designated as the unmanifest. The Knower is the Puruṣa.
These are the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
Among them, *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is solely a cause and not an effect.
The seven [principles] beginning with *mahat* (the Great One) are effects of each preceding one and causes of each succeeding one.
The eleven faculties and the five great elements are only effects and not causes;
the Puruṣa, however, is neither an effect nor a cause.
Thus it has been said: "Root-prakṛti," and so forth.
The Great Principle (mahat) and the five subtle elements (tanmātras)—these seven are both primordial matter (prakṛti) and transformation (vikṛti).

Intellect (buddhi) is born from the Primal Nature (pradhāna), and thus it is a transformation of the Primal Nature; that same intellect produces the I-principle (ahaṅkāra), and thus it is primordial matter. The I-principle is also born from the intellect, and thus it is a transformation; it too produces the eleven organs and the five subtle elements, and thus it is primordial matter.

In this context, the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*) is a modification (*vikṛti*) because it is produced from the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); yet it is the material cause (*prakṛti*) because from it space (*ākāśa*) is produced. Likewise, the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*) is a modification because it is produced from the ego-sense; yet it is the material cause because it produces air (*vāyu*). Similarly, the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*) is a modification because it is produced from the ego-sense; yet it is the material cause because it produces fire (*tejas*).

The subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra) is a modification (vikṛti) because it is born from the ego (ahaṅkāra), yet it is a primal nature (prakṛti) because it produces water. Likewise, the subtle element of smell (gandha-tanmātra) is a modification because it is born from the ego, yet it is a primal nature because it produces the earth.
These five subtle elements (tanmātras) are the subtle causes of the gross elements; and the group of sixteen is the transformation (vikāra).

This group of sixteen consists of the five sense organs, the five action organs, the mind as the eleventh, and the five great elements—all of which are merely transformations and not primal nature (prakṛti).
The meaning is that the Puruṣa, however, is neither of these two.
Valid cognition (pramāṇa) is of three kinds: perception, inference, and verbal testimony.
Among these, perception consists of the five sense organs, such as the ear, which apprehend qualities like sound as they are commonly experienced in the world.
Inference, on the other hand, is that which apprehends objects not present to the senses, such as smoke [which leads to the knowledge of fire].

Sound, first of all, is threefold: that which is the object of the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*), that which is the object of the sense of hearing (*śrotra*), and that which is the object of the mind alone (*buddhimātra*).

Among these, sound delimited by locations such as the throat and palate is the object of the organ of speech, because it is its effect; and sound residing in the ear, separated from the organ of speech by [the medium of] sound-waves, is the object of the sense of hearing, because it is perceived by it. However, words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth are objects of the mind alone, because they are perceivable by the mind alone according to the reasoning to be stated hereafter.
Those very phonemes (*pada*) are called *sphoṭa* because they are the instrument for conveying meaning.

This word (*pada*) is something distinct from each individual phoneme uttered by the organ of speech; for, due to the extremely rapid perishability of phonemes, there is no possibility of their conjunction, and thus it would be impossible for them to be the object of the conventional usage "one word," nor could they possibly be the remembrancer of meaning.

Furthermore, the cause of this *sphoṭa* is a single specific effort (*prayatna-viśeṣa*), since when utterance occurs through a difference in effort, the conventional usage of "one word" does not arise and the cognition of meaning does not occur.
And the manifestor of that *sphoṭa* is the cognition of the final phoneme, qualified by its specific sequence; therefore, it is the cognition itself that grasps the *sphoṭa*.

Since the sequence can be apprehended by the cognition alone, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to hold that the cognition of the sequence—through the proximity of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) alone—is the cause for the manifestation of the word called *sphoṭa*.

For this very reason, the *sphoṭa* cannot be apprehended by the auditory organ; for it is impossible to perceive through the ear a sequence (*ānupūrvī*) that lacks form, such as the state of being "after *gh*" or "after *ṭa*" and so on. Furthermore, because phonemes perish so rapidly, their conjunction is impossible.

Moreover, it is more appropriate that the impressions (*saṃskāra*) and memories of each preceding phoneme—residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—should act as auxiliaries to that same internal organ [rather than to the auditory organ].

It might be argued: let the status of being a word (*padatva*) or the capacity to convey meaning belong solely to the final phoneme as qualified by its specific sequence—which is the manifester of the *sphoṭa*; what is the use of a *sphoṭa*, according to the maxim that "the effect should reside in the very cause of that [effect]"?
This very point has been stated in the Sāṃkhya-sūtra: "Sound is not of the nature of a *sphoṭa*, because of its perception and non-perception [respectively].
Furthermore, the cognition of unity is also explained through the unity of the final phoneme as qualified by its sequence.
To this it is replied: if that were so, it would follow that the whole (avayavin) is annihilated;
for one might as well assume that the parts themselves—constrained by a specific conjunction that serves as the non-inherent cause—are the cause of the fetching of water and so forth.

On account of parsimony (*lāghava*), let that [the sphoṭa] alone be the cause of that [cognition], for the same logic applies: cognitions such as "one jar" are likewise accounted for just like the cognition "one forest.

If it is argued that the proof for the existence of the whole (*avayavin*) is based on the fact that, since atoms and their conjunctions are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the whole would otherwise be impossible—this argument applies equally to the sphoṭa; for if the sphoṭa consists of the final phoneme qualified by a sequence (*ānupūrvī*), then that sequence itself is composed of moments and other imperceptible factors.
The argument that "the perception of a word [as a single unit] is impossible" and so forth serves as a proof for the *sphoṭa*.

Furthermore, we postulate the word *sphoṭa* on the basis of the authority of the Veda (*śruti*) alone, just like heaven (*svarga*) and other such things; therefore, there is no harm even if there is an absence of worldly means of knowledge (*laukikapramāṇa*) regarding it.

For instance, after stating that the three morae (mātrās) of the *praṇava*—namely *a*, *u*, and *m*—are identical with the triad of deities beginning with Brahmā, the Śrutis declare the *praṇava* to be the fourth mora, which consists of the Supreme Brahman transcending the three deities.

That fourth mora can only be the *sphoṭa* itself, which is distinct from the three phonemes; it is this very [sphoṭa] that is called the "half-mora" (*ardhamātrā*). This is because, just as in the case of a heap, when phonemes and words are not yet divided, the phonemes constitute one half and the word constitutes the other half.
And thus it is established that there is another half [of the *mātrā*].

Just as a whole (*avayavin*) cannot be designated in conventional usage when separated from its parts, in exactly the same way, a word (*pada*) cannot be uttered when separated from its individual phonemes (*varṇa*). Therefore, it is recorded in tradition: "The half-*mātrā* remains eternal, which is not to be articulated specifically."
Now, it might be argued that the derivation of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*) is thus established;
however, what is said to be the essential nature of *nāda* and *bindu*?

When the *praṇava* is being uttered, that particular sound which arises—like the resonance of a conch or a flute—is *nāda*. And that extremely subtle state of the cessation of *nāda*, due to its similarity to emptiness (*śūnya*), is called *bindu*.
Thus, it is established that just as a whole (avayavin) is distinct from its parts, so too the word (pada), which is distinct from its constituent phonemes (varṇa), is the sphoṭa.

If it is objected that, in this case, the sentence (vākya) would also be a sphoṭa, we reply: no; provided there is no subverting evidence, let it be accepted—this is the general direction of the argument.
First, "word" (*śabda*) refers to the speech of an authoritative person, such as "Indra is the king of the gods," and so forth.

If presumption (*arthāpatti*), probability (*sambhava*), non-existence (*abhāva*), tradition (*aitihya*), intuition (*pratibhā*), and analogy (*upamāna*) are valid means of knowledge, they must be included within these very [two] and are not separate.
Although *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* exist, they are not perceived due to their subtlety, just as smoke, heat, mist, and atoms exist in the sky but are not perceived despite being present.
By observing effects such as the Mahat and so forth, the Pradhāna is inferred as their cause.

An effect such as the Mahat, produced from the Pradhāna consisting of the three guṇas, is in some respects similar to its material cause (prakṛti) and in some respects similar to its modification (vikṛti), because in the world effects are seen to take two forms, as in the case of a son.
Furthermore, that effect is existent, not non-existent, not both existent and non-existent, and not indefinable; for if it were absolutely non-existent, oil would be produced even from sand.

The other two positions are indeed contradictory: [the first holds that] the unmanifest (*avyakta*), known as *pradhāna*, is independent, all-pervading, and eternal; whereas the manifest (*vyakta*), known as the effect, is dependent, non-pervading, and non-eternal.
The *puruṣa* is independent, all-pervading, and eternal. *Prajāpati* asserts that *pradhāna* is the cause of the three worlds and that it is one for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*).

At the time of dissolution, the effects beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) dissolve into primordial matter (pradhāna). That primordial matter consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; it is the state of equilibrium among these three qualities that constitutes prakṛti.
Pradhāna is insentient, whereas Puruṣa is sentient;
he is distinct from both the manifest and Pradhāna, pure, and devoid of the guṇas.
Since the effect produces pleasure, pain, and delusion, the causes existing therein—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are to be inferred.
And it is observed that, in due order, a woman in love produces pleasure, pain, and delusion in her husband, his rival wife, and her lover respectively.

Even though an effect consists of the three *guṇas*, when *sattva* is predominant due to the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of people, then, having overcome *rajas* and *tamas*, it produces its own effect, which is pleasure.
Likewise, when *rajas* is predominant, then, having overcome *sattva* and *tamas*, it produces its own effect, which is pain.
Thus, when tamas is predominant, it overcomes sattva and rajas and produces its own effect, which is delusion (moha).
Suffering is threefold, distinguished as internal (*ādhyātmika*), external (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*adhidaivika*). To explain: therein, the internal is of two kinds—bodily and mental.
Bodily suffering, for its part, consists of fever, dysentery, and so forth, produced by the imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*).
Mental suffering (*mānasam*), however, arises from separation from the beloved, union with the unpleasant, and so forth.

Suffering caused by living beings (*ādhibhautikam*) is fourfold, originating from the classes of beings: it arises from domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, humans, reptiles, gadflies, lice, bedbugs, and stationary things; that is, from those born from a womb, from eggs, from sweat, and from sprouts.

That which originates from the divine is celestial (*daivam*); that which arises with reference to that [divine] is super-divine (*ādhidaivikam*), such as that born from cold, heat, wind, rain, and the falling of thunderbolts.
Just as threads combined together produce a cloth, so does *pradhāna*— which consists of a collection of qualities (*guṇas*)— generate effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*).

Just as water from the sky, though of a single flavor, acquires a different taste when it falls into a pond or similar body of water due to its contact with that pond, so too, although *pradhāna* is of a single nature, gods and other beings successively become happy, miserable, or utterly deluded.

Likewise, due to the predominance of *sattva* and the indifference of *rajas* and *tamas*, the gods are exceedingly happy; due to the predominance of *rajas* and the indifference of *sattva* and *tamas*, human beings are exceedingly miserable;
and due to the predominance of *tamas* and the indifference of *sattva* and *rajas*, animals are exceedingly deluded.
The aggregate consisting of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest is dependent upon an enjoyer, because it is an object of enjoyment, like a couch;
the aggregate of the Great Principle and the rest is subordinate to another, because it is insentient, like a garland.
In this manner, the Puruṣa is inferred.
And that [multiplicity] arises from the individual distinction of the various instruments of birth and death.
This is the meaning:

if there were only one self, then upon the death of one, all would die; and upon the birth of one, all would be born; and upon the impairment of the instruments of one, all would possess impaired instruments.
And it is not seen to be so; therefore, they are distinct.
From the correct knowledge of the twenty-five principles (tattvas), liberation (kaivalya) occurs for the person (puruṣa).
That distinctness consists in the difference from primordial matter (pradhāna) and the rest; such is the meaning.
From non-discrimination comes transmigratory existence; from discrimination comes liberation.
This implies, by its very meaning, the acceptance of the theory of non-apprehension (akhyāti-vāda).
For this reason, the cognition "this is silver" is not an error, but rather two distinct cognitions that are undiscriminated both in their own form and in their objects.
The conclusion is that for whom this world appears as "this is silver," appearing as the object of that cognition of silver, for him the world is exactly of such a nature.

Therefore, transformation (pariṇāma) is defined by its characteristic as a real, ontological change into another state; such transformation is accepted [in the case of the constituents], whereas the Puruṣa is distinct in every body. Because he is changeless, he is in reality a non-agent, like one who is liberated, indifferent like a witness. It is the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas that are the agents, and they also constitute the actions.
Although the *puruṣa* is not an agent, it is treated as if it were an agent;
just as one who is not a thief is regarded as a thief when seized along with thieves.
Due to the non-differentiation of qualities (*guṇa*), it is *prakṛti* that is the agent, not the *puruṣa*.

The conjunction of the *puruṣa*, who possesses the power of vision but lacks the power of action, with *pradhāna*— in order for *pradhāna* to be seen from the stage of the *mahat* down to the gross elements— and likewise the conjunction of *pradhāna*, which lacks the power of vision but possesses the power of action, with the *puruṣa*— is for the sake of liberation. When knowledge of the distinctness of the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the *puruṣa* has arisen, liberation occurs for both *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*.

If it is argued that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the attainment of eternal happiness, this is unsubstantial because even such an attainment is consumed by the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal.

Nor can it be said that the mere removal of some obscuration—such as ignorance (*avidyā*)—regarding the object of eternal happiness constitutes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), for the experience of happiness itself is the human goal; furthermore, since consciousness is eternal, the existence of any obscuration is impossible.

As for the scriptural and traditional texts proclaiming supreme bliss in liberation, they are merely technical conventions of the treatises on liberation. Since there is only suffering and no pleasure because that [pleasure] is perceived [only] as such, the designation "pleasure" is applied to the remedy for one afflicted by suffering.
Dependence on sensual pleasure is suffering; the transcendence of suffering is known as happiness.

By such Smṛti passages, the cessation of suffering alone is designated as happiness. The Sāṃkhya Sūtra also states: "The cessation of suffering is the primary [goal]," and "The praise of liberation for the dull-witted is secondary.

Furthermore, the attainment of bliss occurs in the world of Brahmā as a secondary form of liberation; subsequently, there occurs a separation of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, who have accomplished their purposes, like the parting of the blind man and the lame man.
For instance, there was one who was lame and another who was blind; both of them, traveling on a dangerous path with a great caravan, were by chance abandoned by their kinsmen.
Deprived respectively of the power of movement and the power of sight, they became joined together for the purpose of seeing and for the purpose of going.
Thus, it is like a blind man who has placed a lame man upon his shoulders; the blind man travels along the path shown by him, and the lame man, mounted upon the blind man's shoulders, also travels.
Afterwards, once they have each reached their own respective destinations and achieved their purpose, they become separated.
In the same way, primordial matter (*pradhāna*), having accomplished the liberation of the spirit (*puruṣa*), ceases its activity.
The *puruṣa* neither engages in activity nor desists from it;
the *puruṣa* is the seer and the enjoyer. Enjoyment is characterized by its termination in consciousness (*cit*).
That Puruṣa is not essentially characterized by the immersion in activity; yet, due to beginningless non-discrimination (aviveka), he transmigrates.
Through hearing the true scriptures and by the grace of the Guru, when doubt is dispelled and discriminative knowledge arises, he is liberated.
From the conjunction of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) is produced.
Just as offspring arises from the union of a woman and a man, the principle of Mahat is born from Prakṛti.
From the principle of Mahat, Ahaṅkāra is born;
and it is of three kinds: Vaikārika, Bhūtādi, and Taijasa.
For that which is *vaikārika* is itself *sāttvika*; that which is *bhūtādi* is itself *tāmasa*;

and that which is *taijasa* is itself *rājasa*. From the *vaikārika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the eleven organs and the deities presiding over them are born. From the *bhūtādi* ego, the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are born. And from the *taijasa* ego, both the group of eleven organs and the pentad of subtle elements are born.
If it is asked how the production of these two groups is described again— since they have already arisen respectively from the *vaikārika* and the *bhūtādi* forms of *ahaṃkāra*—
listen: when the *sattva* quality, having overcome *rajas* and *tamas*, becomes predominant and acquires the name *vaikārika*, that *ahaṃkāra*, being of the nature of non-activity,
takes the *taijasa* *ahaṃkāra* as its assistant and generates the eleven organs, which are of the nature of activity.
Then, it is said that those [five subtle elements] are produced even by the Taijasa [ego], having obtained its assistance through a form of deception.
And when the Bhūtādi [ego], with the quality of Tamas predominant, overcomes Sattva and Rajas, and taking the form of the Taijasa ego as its aid,
produces the group of five subtle elements (tanmātras) characterized by activity, then that group of five subtle elements exists solely through its own assistance.

It is said that [the gross elements] are also produced by the Taijasa [aspect]; therefore, from those five subtle elements (tanmātra) characterized by the quality of activity (pravṛttidharma), the five gross elements arise.
This is the sequence of transformation:
from the Vaikārika [aspect] come the eleven organs, and from the Bhūtādi [aspect] comes the pentad of subtle elements.
This is the meaning:

in the production of their respective two types of effects—characterized by the quality of *pravṛtti* (activity)—which belong to the *vaikārika* and the *bhūtādi* [forms of ego], the *taijasa* ego-constituent provides assistance according to their respective order.
It is precisely because the *taijasa* ego-constituent renders such assistance that these two groups of effects possess the quality of *pravṛtti*.
The sense organs that produce cognition are the cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriyāṇi*); these are the sense organs of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.
And their objects are form, sound, odor, flavor, and tangibility.
Those which perform actions are the active faculties (*karmendriyāṇi*); and these are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ.
And their objects are speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure.

The mind (*manas*) is both a faculty of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) and a faculty of action (*karmendriya*), because it conceives the activity of the cognitive faculties and that of the active faculties; therefore, the mind possesses the nature of both.

Furthermore, the mind is all-pervasive (*vibhu*); as the substratum for the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of merit and demerit, it is an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) for each individual soul and is eternal like space.

Nor should it be said that *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) and the like are simply properties of the primordial matter (*prakṛti*), because if pleasure, pain, and so forth were produced in one place by an *adṛṣṭa* residing in another, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, that [perception] is not possible for an atom, since it is impossible for a yogi to have direct perception of everything simultaneously through every part [of his body].

Nor can the property born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) itself be the means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) for yogis; for when the perception is already established through ordinary means of contact such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*), there is no evidence for postulating an additional sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*).
Furthermore, there is excessive complexity (*gaurava*) and mutual inconsistency (*anyonyavyabhicāra*).
If one were to postulate intermediate universals (*avāntarajāti*) for direct perceptions, there would be a confusion of universals (*jātisāṅkarya*) and extreme complexity.

According to the Yoga school, since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is capable of grasping all objects, it is simply the removal of the veil called *tamas* by means of *yogaja-dharma* and other factors [that constitutes perception].

It is established that in deep sleep, darkness (tamas) acts as an obstacle to the functioning [of the internal organ]; nor is it possible for the internal organ to possess merely a medium size, because its destruction at the time of dissolution would render it impossible to serve as the substratum for unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and the like. Therefore, by the method of elimination, the internal organ is established as being indeed all-pervading (vibhu). Thus it has been said:
There is the space of the mind (*cittākāśa*), the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), and the third is [ordinary] space (*ākāśa*).
Know, O fair-faced one, that the space of consciousness is the emptiest of the two.
It might be argued as follows:

even if the all-pervasiveness of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is accepted, and its acquisition of a limited function is explained by means of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), such things as traveling to other worlds would still be untenable.
For this very reason, the Sāṃkhya Sūtra states: "The mind is not all-pervasive, because it is an instrument (*karaṇatvāt*)."

Regarding the phrase "or because of the scriptural statement of its movement": furthermore, this being the case, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more appropriate to postulate an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) of consciousness itself; why then is an all-pervasive internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) postulated, and an obscuration that obstructs knowledge attributed to it?
To this it is replied:

First, as for the scriptural mention of "going," it is possible even for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—just as it is for the self—due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the senses, because of the duality of the internal organ in the form of cause and effect.

Furthermore, movement is possible for the "effect-internal-organ" (*kāryāntaḥkaraṇa*) by its own nature as well. Moreover, the Sāṃkhyas must also accept a duality of the internal organ in the form of cause and effect; for if it were merely an effect, [qualities] would belong only to the internal organ.
The phrase "of dharma and so forth" is untenable according to the Sāṃkhya sūtras;

and if there were absolute permanence, the sūtra concerning the production of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest would be untenable. As for the claim that it is more reasonable to postulate an obscuration of consciousness itself, that is incorrect, because an obscuration in the form of an impediment to knowledge is impossible for immutable consciousness.

Nor should it be argued that the very relation of consciousness with an object must be postulated as the obstacle to its appearing in the form of a reflection and so forth; for even so, the perception of the self would remain unaccounted for, since without the mediation of an instrument, a relation with itself in the form of a reflection and so forth is impossible.

Moreover, once the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is established as the substratum of desire, volition, and so forth, even the jars and other objects perceived internally during dreams are postulated to be its own transformations (*pariṇāma*), because it is appropriate that cause and effect share a common locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Thus, when consciousness manifests in the form of a jar or the like, external jars and such appear precisely through non-distinction from that [internal transformation]; therefore, it is logical that the obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) which obstructs such a transformation must reside in that very [internal organ]. Furthermore, by observing obscuration in the case of the external organs, [one infers] the existence of internal obscuration as well.
Furthermore, the fact that the self is not veiled is inferred from its being established as the locus of the instruments [of action], as well as from Śruti and Smṛti.

Now, one might object: "If the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) were all-pervading (*vibhu*), how could it possess the nature of an effect? This is not so; for just as the material cause of space (*ākāśa-prakṛti*), though all-pervading, undergoes a transformation into the limited form of the effected space (*kāryākāśa*) through the intermingling of other qualities, so too the material cause of the internal organ can undergo a transformation into the limited form of the internal organ through the intermingling of other qualities.
This is accepted because of the authority of the Śruti and Smṛti; such is the direction [of the argument].
The object of the mind is volition (*saṅkalpa*).

It has been stated that these eleven [senses] are born from the modified ego (*vaikṛta-ahaṃkāra*). Thus, the person (*puruṣa*) perceives the object reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*). As it is said: "The person is conscious of the object situated in the intellect."
The determination that "I shall perform dharma" is the characteristic of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Dharma, knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*virāga*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)—these belong to the intellect characterized by *sattva*. That which is the opposite of these, such as lack of dispassion and so forth, belongs to the *tāmasa* intellect.

The universe is pervaded by exactly twenty-five principles, neither fewer nor more; just as milk flows for the sake of the calf's growth, so too is the activity of the *pradhāna*, though it is insentient, appropriate for the sake of the liberation of the *puruṣa*.

The subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), however, is a collection of eighteen constituents—the intellect, ego, mind, the five sense organs, the five organs of action, and the five subtle elements—formed by excluding the five gross elements from the twenty-three principles and merging the ego into the intellect.

The seventeen-fold entity is known as the *liṅga-śarīra* (subtle body), because it serves as the locus for the manifestation of the Self, just as fuel is for fire. This [subtle body] arises at the beginning of creation for all persons and persists until the dissolution of primordial nature (*prākṛta-pralaya*). Through this very [subtle body], the transmigratory wandering (*saṃsaraṇa*) of living beings occurs between this world and the next. Furthermore, since vital breath (*prāṇa*) is merely a specific modification (*vṛtti-bheda*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), it is not mentioned separately from the subtle body; and of that [subtle body]...

The subtle elements of the five gross elements constitute the substrate of the *liṅgaśarīra*, like a canvas for a painting; for without such a substrate, it is impossible for that which is supremely subtle to travel to another world.

And this subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) is first produced as a single entity, serving as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the Self-born (svayaṃbhū), just like the gross body (sthūla-śarīra) called Virāṭ which is to be described later.
Thereafter, the individual subtle bodies (vyaṣṭi-liṅga-śarīras), which serve as the limiting adjuncts for individual souls (jīvas) and are constituent parts of that [original one],
become differentiated from it, just as the subtle body of a son is differentiated from the subtle body of the father.
This was stated by the author of the Sūtras:
"The distinction of individual manifestations arises from the difference in karma. Manu has also said:
"Of those six [elements], which possess immeasurable power, the subtle constituent parts..."
"Having placed [the elements] within the portions of the Self (ātma-mātrā), He created all beings.

Regarding the word "of the six," this refers to the six sense organs as indicative of the entire subtle body (liṅga-śarīra). Thus, the meaning is that Svayambhū, having joined the minute and subtle limbs of His own subtle body with the portions of the Self—that is, with His own constituent conscious principles—created all living beings; such is the subtle body.

As for the production of the gross body: within the tenfold-magnified *mahat-tattva*, the *ahaṃkāra* arises; within that tenfold-magnified [ahaṃkāra], space (*vyoman*); within that tenfold-magnified space, air (*vāyu*); within that tenfold-magnified air, fire (*tejas*); within that tenfold-magnified fire, water (*jala*); and within that tenfold-magnified water, earth (*pṛthivī*) is produced.

That very [subtle body] is the seed of the gross body, and that same seed, in the form of earth, transforms into the form of an egg; in the midst of that covering of earth, which consists of tenfold eggs, the gross body of Svayambhū— comprising the fourteen worlds— is produced solely through his volition, and by means of that very body, Svayambhū is called Nārāyaṇa.
This has been stated by Manu with reference to the Self-existent One (Svayambhū):
"Desiring to emit various creatures, he, having meditated, first created water alone;
into that he cast his seed."
Then there arose a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun;
within that sacrificial vessel was Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.
He is indeed the first embodied being; he is called the Puruṣa. He is the original creator of all beings; as Brahmā, he existed at the beginning.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of *nara*;
since they were his primordial abode (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Regarding the phrase "by such passages as this":

because the individual persons (*vyaṣṭipuruṣa*) originate from that very First Person (*ādipuruṣa*), and because they are ultimately dissolved back into Him, He alone is designated as the "One Self" (*eka ātmā*) in both Śruti and Smṛti. Therefore, since these texts are intended for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), there is no contradiction with Śruti and Smṛti passages stating that Nārāyaṇa alone is the Self of all beings and so forth.

Then that Nārāyaṇa, possessing the body of Virāṭ, having created upon Mount Sumeru—which serves as the pericarp of his own navel-lotus—the self-born one named Caturmukha (the Four-faced), through him created all other individual embodied beings down to the level of stationary objects; as it has been said:
"Together with those effects and causes produced from his body..."
"Kṣetrajñas were born from the limbs of that wise one.

As for the scriptural account of the manifestation of the four-faced Brahmā from the navel-lotus, ears, eyes, and other organs of Nārāyaṇa reclining on Śeṣa, that should be understood as occurring only during the daily creations according to the distinctions between Kalpas;

for it is precisely during the daily dissolutions that the gods, having entered and become one with the body of Nārāyaṇa and slept there, manifest again in the sequence beginning with the four-faced one.

This is possible from Him who reclines upon Śeṣa during the daily dissolution (dainandinapralaya), but not during the primordial creations (ādisarga), because He reclines there only in a sport-form (līlāvigraha).

Thus, in brief, the twenty-four principles (*tattva*), their creation and dissolution, and their purpose have been explained. In this regard, that from which something is born exists by being filled by that very thing; therefore, its dissolution also occurs in that same place.
And so it is said in the *Mahābhārata*:
"Whatever reality is born from something, that dissolves back into it;
things dissolve in reverse order and are born in successive order."

These gross transformations of the twenty-four principles, consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, have been demonstrated for the sake of discriminating them from the immutable Puruṣa; however, other subtle transformations occurring at every moment are also recorded in the Smṛti:
"The limbs of the body are constantly being born and perishing."
"Because its velocity is imperceptible due to its subtlety, it is not grasped.
Therefore, every insentient object is said to be ultimately non-existent at all times.
Consequently, having become detached from that, those who fear suffering should perceive the Self alone as the ultimate reality; as it has been said:
The great tree has its origin in the seed of the Unmanifest;
it consists of the trunk of the intellect, has the great ego as its branches, and the sense organs as the hollows of its sprouts.
It has the great elements as its main branches and the specific [elements] as its twigs;
it is always leafy, always flowering, and yields the fruit of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
The eternal Brahma-tree is the livelihood of all beings;
having known this in its true essence through the supreme sword of knowledge, [one is liberated].
"Having attained the state of the Imperishable, one abandons birth and death.
Thus it is said:
"Therefore, indeed, the senses and the objects of the senses no longer approach him."
And the embodied soul, being deficient in its instruments, does not deserve a body again.

"Therefore, all living beings are born from passion (rāga) which consists of all [afflictions]. Thus, even though there is an absence of specific passion (*viśeṣarāga*) in the hells and other such realms, because general passion (*sāmānyarāga*) exists, passion acts as a cooperative condition for karma at the commencement of its fruition. This is stated in the Śruti: "Attached to that very [object], he goes together with his karma; where his mind is fastened, there is his subtle body (*liṅga*)," referring to that which is produced by self-conceit, passion, hatred, and so forth.
This is because it is established that the common factor known as attachment to latent impressions (*vāsanā*) serves as the auxiliary cause for the commencement of the fruition of birth and so forth;
as the Smṛti states: "In whatever object the embodied one holds his mind with his intellect—whether out of affection, aversion, or even attraction—he attains the very form of that [object]."
Thus, with his eyes turned back and awakened by the mirror of the Guru,
he immediately perceived through his own delusion a transformation other than himself that was not actually present.
Then, realizing "I am not this primordial nature (prakṛti), for it is defiled by essence; I am of the nature of pure awakening," one abandons it.
Thus, when the Self is remembered as pure in contrast to the body, senses, and so forth,
this entire world of modifications is indeed cast off like a piece of skin.

If it is asked: "How can ignorance, which consists of the notion of a self in what is not-self, be destroyed by the discriminative knowledge that has the self as its qualificand, given the difference in their respective modes (prakāra) and other factors?"—the answer is no; for such ignorance is destroyed by discriminative knowledge having the self as its qualificand through the mediation of discriminative knowledge having the non-self as its qualificand. Furthermore, through yoga, there arises a non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka) knowledge of the self.

That [knowledge] becomes the cause of liberation only through the door of discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*), and not directly; for it lacks the capacity to remove ignorance (*avidyā*). Indeed, the cognition "I am fair-complexioned, an agent, happy, or miserable" is established by *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and reasoning as being ignorance itself, since it is the cause of the misfortune of *saṃsāra*. And the remover of that [ignorance] is precisely discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) in the form "I am not fair-complexioned," and so forth.
When the object is the same, there is opposition precisely because the cognition of the absence of the apprehended object has the "absence of the apprehended object" as its qualifier;
otherwise, even the non-conceptual cognition of liberation would result in being opposed to the cognition "this is silver.

Furthermore, since the opposition to the cognition of the apprehended object is necessary in the case of the aforementioned cognition of absence, the capacity of non-conceptual cognition to remove error is not postulated separately, due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*).

Moreover, it is said that there is no instruction superior to the instruction of discrimination, according to such scriptural passages as: "Now, therefore, the teaching is 'not this, not this' (neti neti); for there is nothing higher than this 'not this'"; and so forth.
Thus, those who perceive with the eye of knowledge the distinction between the field and the knower of the field, as well as the liberation from the material nature of beings, attain the Supreme.

Thus, by these verses from the *Gītā*, it is stated that discriminative knowledge alone is the cause of liberation; therefore, discriminative knowledge itself is the direct cause of liberation through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*).

As for the direct realization of the Self (*ātman*) through yoga, it brings about the cessation of ignorance by apprehending—by way of non-perception of the capable—the absence of attributes residing in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and the distinction between those adjuncts.

Consequently, the knowledge of equality among all beings and the knowledge of the Self as being the Self of all, which are extolled in the Śruti and Smṛti, should be understood in all philosophical systems as being subsidiary to discriminative knowledge itself.

Since other forms of knowledge do not directly eliminate the sense of ego (abhimāna), there is this distinction in the Brahma-mīmāṃsā: that its purpose culminates in the discrimination of the Supreme Self (paramātman);
whereas in the Sāṃkhya system, its purpose culminates in the discrimination of the general self (sāmānyātman). This is the direction of the argument.

Discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), however, functions solely as the destroyer of ignorance; it does not act as an obstacle in the manner of one who perceives the distinction between mother-of-pearl and silver, for whom delusion may recur due to a multitude of defects such as cataracts or other ocular ailments—as is the case with the example where delusion is revived. In this context, regarding the conceit of self in what is not-self, the defect is universally accepted by all proponents of existence (*sarvāstika*) to be nothing other than beginningless latent impressions (*anādivāsanā*), given that such conceit arises even in one who has just been born.

Since no other defect is perceived, that latent impression (*vāsanā*) of false knowledge is said to reach the culmination of discriminative discernment (*viveka-sākṣātkāra*) precisely when it is uprooted by the firm impression produced by the continuous stream of discriminative discernment. Prior to that, some portion of the false must necessarily appear within the self due to a remnant of the impression;
however, once this culmination of discriminative discernment has arisen, further egoistic conceit (*abhimāna*) is impossible because of the absence of the defect known as the impression.

If, however, the mutual reflection between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*), and so forth, is accepted as a defect that causes non-discrimination (*aviveka*), then the direct realization of discrimination (*vivekasākṣātkāra*) has arisen precisely by subduing that defect; therefore, it cannot again be the cause of error, because— by the force of the result—
it is only when that [reflection] is not assisted by the merit born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) that its status as a defect can be postulated.
Although it is impossible to grasp discrimination (*viveka*) in its specific form because the objects that serve as the counter-correlates of discrimination are infinite, nevertheless,

since it is possible to grasp discrimination in a general sense through such forms as "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*) or "undergoing transformation" (*pariṇāmitva*), the discernment of discrimination (*vivekakhyāti*) in a general manner— even in the absence of specific knowledge of categories such as *prakṛti*— is the cause of liberation.
As it has been said:

"Just as the perceiver of a jar is in every way distinct from the jar, so too the embodied self (dehī) is the perceiver of the body; [it is not the body] by virtue of such forms as 'I am not [the body]' and so forth."

In the statement "The Self, indeed, is to be seen," however, the Self does not possess the quality of being an object of vision in the sense of being pervaded by the fruit [of cognition], even though it is pervaded by the mental modification (*vṛtti*).
For instance, even when the intellect is experienced by the Buddhists as possessing pleasure, pain, and so forth, it is not pervaded by consciousness (*caitanya*) by virtue of its self-luminosity;
likewise, for the Vedāntins, although the Self is experienced as "I," it is not pervaded by the fruit called consciousness.
It is said that [the self] exists; however, because it lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that claim should be disregarded.

It is produced during the primary creation (*pradhāna-ādi-sarga*) and transmigrates through animals and the like by the power of non-dharma (*adharma*), and through gods and the like by the power of dharma (*dharma*).

Precisely because of the lack of knowledge of reality (*atattvajñāna*), that which is colored by merit and demerit (*dharmādharmoparañjita*) dissolves into primordial matter (*pradhāna*) at the time of dissolution.
Although both primordial matter and the spirit (*puruṣa*) are all-pervading (*vibhu*), nevertheless, it is primordial matter alone that establishes the subtle body (*liṅga*).
This subtle body, accumulated from subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), persists among humans and other beings, just like an actor.

Just as an actor, though being one in his true nature, appears in various forms through different costumes, so too the subtle body (*liṅga*), having entered within the womb, becomes an elephant, a woman, or a man; thus there arise the five types of delusion (*viparyaya*), namely: darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*moha*), great delusion (*mahāmoha*), gloom (*tāmisra*), and utter gloom (*andhatāmisra*).
Through merit (*dharma*), one attains the higher worlds, beginning with that of Prajāpati.
Through unrighteousness one obtains cattle and the like; through ignorance comes bondage; and through knowledge of the twenty-five principles (tattvas) comes liberation.
That knowledge of the principles arises from hearing the scriptures in the presence of a teacher as follows:

the Puruṣa is distinct from Pradhāna; the intellect (buddhi) is distinct; the ego (ahaṃkāra) is distinct; and the subtle elements (tanmātras), the sense organs, and the five gross elements are each distinct.

Every effect, although composed of the three *guṇas*, receives designations such as "sāttvika" and so forth in accordance with its predominant *guṇa*. The conscious *puruṣa* experiences the suffering caused by old age and death within various wombs;
as long as the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) is not dissolved through the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), the gross body is produced anew and perishes at every birth.
Even in the absence of any purpose for itself, *pradhāna*—from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the objects of perception—acts like a good friend, independent of any return favor.

Nature (prakṛti) undertakes activity for the sake of the experience and liberation of the person (puruṣa); having manifested intellect, ego, and so forth through its differentiation from the person, it desists.

Just as a dancer, having exhibited songs and the like composed with sentiments such as the erotic and emotions such as the comic on the stage, desists because her purpose has been fulfilled, so too does Nature.

Furthermore, Nature (prakṛti), which possesses qualities, assists the qualityless Spirit (puruṣa)— who is otherwise unassisted— by acting as the source of the world through her nature consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, or by assuming the form of objects such as sound and so forth; having thus assisted the Spirit and subsequently revealed herself, she desists, thinking "I am one, you are another," like a good friend, and does not desire any recompense from the Spirit.
The Lord is not the cause of creation, nor is it inherent nature (*svabhāva*), nor is it time (*kāla*). For yogis, time consists solely of moments (*kṣaṇa*);

it is not—as held by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas—an indivisible, eternal, and unitary entity like the self (*ātman*). Rather, by parsimony (*lāghava*), it is that very [time] which, being delimited by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), performs the conventional transactions from a moment and a muhūrta up to a year.
But there is no separate category of entity called a "moment."

The Sāṃkhyas, however, have formulated in their aphorism that [time] arises from space, time, ether, and so forth; they maintain that there is no separate category of reality such as "Great Time" (*mahākāla*) or "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) and the like, but rather that it is space itself, as qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that produces the conventional designations ranging from the moment to Great Time.
The Yogi states that both of these views are untenable, because the conventional usage of "moment" cannot arise from either Great Time or space through any stable limiting adjunct whatsoever.

For instance, others maintain that the motion of an atom or the like, as delimited by conjunction with a northern location, or some other such thing, serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the momentary nature of Great Time (*mahākāla*) and Space (*ākāśa*). Regarding this, it has been stated: if [the adjunct] consists of motion qualified by conjunction and so forth, then—since the three factors (the qualified, the qualifier, and their relation) are admitted by others to be permanent—it would not be possible to account for the conventional usage of "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) on their basis. If...

And that [moment] is not held to be something distinct from them; nor is it Mahākāla or Ākāśa, because since the conventional usage of "moment" is established by those very [factors], it would be redundant to postulate another entity delimited by them as the cause of the convention "moment.

Furthermore, this moment—whether characterized as a specific state (*viśiṣṭa*) or otherwise—is not stable, but is simply an extremely transitory particular transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) of Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) itself; therefore, there is no consequence of its being something distinct from both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.
Through specific accumulations of that very moment, there arises the conventional usage of "muhūrta," "day and night," and so forth, up to the limit of the "two half-parārdhas";

however, there is no such thing as an indivisible, great time (*mahākāla*), because there is a lack of evidence. Conventional usages such as "today" and so on occur solely through the accumulation of moments. As for the Śruti and Smṛti texts concerning the eternity of time, they refer instead to the eternity of the continuous flow (*pravāha*). Therefore, since it is necessary, time consists only of moments; there is no indivisible, great time.
Nor is space the cause of the conventional usage of time; rather, it is primordial matter (pradhāna).

It is not the person (puruṣa) who is bound, nor liberated, nor does he transmigrate; rather, it is primordial matter alone, depending on various substrates, that acts in such ways—thus everything is consistent.
Thus ends the *Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana*, composed by the illustrious Śrī Ṣimānandadīkṣita of Kānyakubja.
